title: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time
summary: The stack is fast but small, and everything on it disappears when its function returns. For data whose size or lifetime is only known at run time (a level loaded from disk, a list of bullets), programs ask the **heap** for memory. This lesson shows how `new`, `delete`, smart pointers and containers use it, what it costs, and what a Debug build does to help you catch heap mistakes.
markdown:
## Why a second kind of memory Stack memory has two limits: 1. **Its lifetime is tied to a function call.** A local disappears when its function returns. A level loaded inside `loadLevel` must outlive `loadLevel`. 2. **Its size is fixed when the program is compiled.** The compiler must know how big a frame is. A level whose size is read from a file cannot be a local array. The **heap** answers both. It is a large area of the process's memory managed by an **allocator**: you ask for a number of bytes at run time, it finds a free block and gives you its address, and the block stays yours until you give it back. | | Stack | Heap | |---|---|---| | Size decided | At compile time | At run time | | Lifetime | Until the function returns | Until you free it | | Speed of getting memory | One subtraction from `rsp` | A search through the allocator's free blocks | | Typical capacity | 1 MB per thread | Gigabytes, limited by the system | | Freed by | Returning | `delete`, a smart pointer, or a container | ## new and delete `new` asks the heap for room for an object, constructs it there and returns a pointer. `delete` destroys the object and gives the memory back. ```cpp #include struct Monster { int health; int damage; }; int main() { Monster* boss{ new Monster{ 500, 40 } }; // lives on the heap std::cout << "boss has " << boss->health << " health\n"; boss->health -= 120; std::cout << "boss has " << boss->health << " health\n"; delete boss; // gives the memory back boss = nullptr; // the old address is no longer valid int count{ 5 }; int* scores{ new int[count]{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 } }; // an array sized at run time std::cout << "third score " << scores[2] << '\n'; delete[] scores; // arrays need delete[] return 0; } ``` ``` boss has 500 health boss has 380 health third score 30 ``` The pointer `boss` itself is a local on the stack. The `Monster` it points at is on the heap. When `main` returns, the pointer disappears, but the `Monster` would not: if nobody calls `delete`, its memory stays reserved until the process exits. That is a **memory leak**. ## Don't use raw new and delete in modern code Every `new` needs exactly one matching `delete`, on every path through the program, including early returns and exceptions. That is hard to get right by hand, so modern C++ gives the job to objects that free memory in their destructors. ```cpp #include #include #include struct Monster { int health; int damage; }; int main() { // One object, one owner: freed automatically when boss goes out of scope. std::unique_ptr boss{ std::make_unique(Monster{ 500, 40 }) }; std::cout << "boss: " << boss->health << '\n'; // Many objects: the vector owns a heap block and grows it as needed. std::vector wave; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 4; ++i) wave.push_back(Monster{ 50 + i * 10, 5 }); std::cout << "wave of " << wave.size() << ", last has " << wave.back().health << '\n'; return 0; } // wave and boss free their heap memory here ``` ``` boss: 500 wave of 4, last has 80 ``` `std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr` all use the heap underneath. Lesson 2.04 explains the rule that makes this safe (**RAII**), and lesson 3.07 opens up `std::vector` to show exactly how it manages its block. ## What an allocation costs Asking the heap for memory is not free. The allocator has to find a suitable free block, split it, record that it is in use, and later merge it back when it is freed. Each allocation also carries hidden bookkeeping bytes beside it. Games care about this because they run the same code sixty or more times a second. Allocating a few objects at start-up costs nothing noticeable. Allocating thousands of small objects every frame (every bullet, every particle, every temporary string) adds up to real time and scatters data across memory, which is slow to read. Common answers, which later lessons build: - **Reserve up front.** `vector.reserve(1000)` gets one block big enough for the whole wave. - **Reuse.** Keep dead objects in a **pool** and recycle them instead of freeing (lesson 3.10). - **Arenas.** Grab one large block per frame or per level and hand out pieces of it by moving a pointer along, then release the whole block at once. This is the practice task for this lesson. ## Where heap memory comes from On Windows, `new` calls the C runtime's `malloc`, which uses a **heap** managed by Windows itself (the functions `HeapAlloc` and `HeapFree` in `kernel32.dll`). The heap in turn gets large regions of memory from the operating system a page at a time with `VirtualAlloc`, which chapter 6 covers. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["new Monster"] --> B["operator new / malloc
(C runtime)"] B --> C["HeapAlloc
(Windows heap)"] C --> D["VirtualAlloc
(pages from the OS)"] ``` Most of the time only the top of that chain matters. The bottom of it matters when you look at memory in a debugger, because it explains why heap addresses look different from stack addresses. ## What a Debug build does to the heap In a Debug build, Microsoft's C runtime wraps every allocation with extra checks and fills memory with recognisable patterns. Learn them: you will see them constantly in the Memory window. | Byte pattern | Meaning | |---|---| | `CD CD CD CD` | Heap memory that was allocated but not yet written ("clean") | | `DD DD DD DD` | Heap memory that has been freed ("dead"). Reading it means you used a pointer after `delete`. | | `FD FD FD FD` | Guard bytes ("no man's land") placed just before and after each block. If they change, something wrote past the end. | | `CC CC CC CC` | Uninitialised **stack** memory (lesson 1.07) | When you `delete` a block, the Debug runtime checks its guard bytes. If you wrote one element past the end of a `new int[5]`, it notices and stops the program with a "HEAP CORRUPTION DETECTED" message naming the block. Release builds do none of this, which is why heap bugs often "only happen in Release": they were there all along, just not caught. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] new[] with delete, or new with delete[] > Arrays made with `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`. Mixing them is undefined behaviour. The simplest fix is to use `std::vector` instead. > [!warning] Using a pointer after delete > The memory may be handed out again for something else. Set raw pointers to `nullptr` after deleting, or better, use `std::unique_ptr`. > [!warning] Allocating in the hot loop > Building a temporary `std::string` or `std::vector` inside per-frame code allocates every frame. Hoist it out of the loop and reuse it, or reserve once. > [!warning] Thinking a leak is harmless because the program ends > Games run for hours. A few bytes leaked per frame is megabytes per hour, and leaks inside long-running servers or tools eventually exhaust memory. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Name two reasons to put data on the heap instead of the stack. + Its size is known only at run time, or it must outlive its function - It is used often, or it needs to be fast to reach - It is a struct, or it contains pointers - It is read-only, or it is shared between files > Very large data also belongs on the heap because the stack is small. Heap memory is not faster than the stack; it is usually slower to get. ? What is a memory leak? - Reading memory past the end of an array - Using memory after it has been freed + Heap memory that is never freed once it is no longer needed - A local variable that is never used > The memory stays reserved until the process ends. Reading past an array is an overrun, and using freed memory is use-after-free. ? What do the Debug heap patterns `CD`, `DD` and `FD` mean? - `CD` is freed, `DD` is a guard area, `FD` is allocated but unwritten - `CD` is code, `DD` is data, `FD` is a free block - `CD` is uninitialised stack, `DD` is uninitialised heap, `FD` is freed + `CD` is allocated but not yet written, `DD` is freed, `FD` is the guard area around each block > The `FD` guard bytes detect writes past either end of a block. Seeing `DD` through a pointer means the memory has already been freed. ? What is an arena allocator? - An allocator that gives every object its own page of memory + One large block from which pieces are handed out by moving an offset forward, reset all at once - A heap that frees each object automatically when it is last used - A list of free blocks searched for the best fit on each allocation > Individual pieces are never freed; the whole block is reset at once, for example at the end of a frame or level. That is why it is so cheap. ? A level's size is read from a file when the game starts. Where should its tile data go? - In a local array inside `loadLevel` + On the heap, for example in a `std::vector` - In the shadow space > Its size is only known at run time and it must outlive the function that loads it. Both point to the heap. ? In a Debug build, you look at a pointer's target and see `DD DD DD DD`. What has happened? - The memory was allocated but never written - Something wrote past the end of the block + The memory was freed, but is still being used > `DD` is the Debug heap's "dead memory" fill, written when a block is freed. ? Why do games avoid allocating many small objects every frame? - The heap only allows a fixed number of allocations + Each allocation costs time and scatters data, and it adds up - Small objects must go on the stack > Allocation is a search plus bookkeeping. Reserving, pooling and arenas avoid repeating it every frame. ? What frees the memory owned by a `std::vector` local? - You must call `delete` on it - The operating system, when the program exits + The vector's destructor, when the vector goes out of scope > Containers and smart pointers free their heap memory in their destructors. That is the RAII idea in lesson 2.04. ```
ideas:
- In Visual Studio, put a breakpoint after `new Monster{ 500, 40 }`, and type `boss` into the Memory window. Find `F4 01 00 00` (500) and `28 00 00 00` (40). Look just before and after the eight bytes for the `FD` guard bytes.
- Step over `delete boss;` and watch the same bytes turn into `DD`.
- Change `new int[count]` to hold 5 elements and write `scores[5] = 1;` before the `delete[]`. Run the Debug build and read the message.

cards.q: Name two reasons to put data on the heap instead of the stack.
cards.a:
Its size is known only at run time, or it must outlive its function

Very large data also belongs on the heap because the stack is small. Heap memory is not faster than the stack; it is usually slower to get.

Heap memory that is never freed once it is no longer needed

The memory stays reserved until the process ends. Reading past an array is an overrun, and using freed memory is use-after-free.

cards.q: What do the Debug heap patterns `CD`, `DD` and `FD` mean?
cards.a:
`CD` is allocated but not yet written, `DD` is freed, `FD` is the guard area around each block

The `FD` guard bytes detect writes past either end of a block. Seeing `DD` through a pointer means the memory has already been freed.

One large block from which pieces are handed out by moving an offset forward, reset all at once

Individual pieces are never freed; the whole block is reset at once, for example at the end of a frame or level. That is why it is so cheap.

cards.q: A level's size is read from a file when the game starts. Where should its tile data go?
cards.a:
On the heap, for example in a `std::vector`

Its size is only known at run time and it must outlive the function that loads it. Both point to the heap.

cards.q: In a Debug build, you look at a pointer's target and see `DD DD DD DD`. What has happened?
cards.a:
The memory was freed, but is still being used

`DD` is the Debug heap's "dead memory" fill, written when a block is freed.

cards.q: Why do games avoid allocating many small objects every frame?
cards.a:
Each allocation costs time and scatters data, and it adds up

Allocation is a search plus bookkeeping. Reserving, pooling and arenas avoid repeating it every frame.

cards.q: What frees the memory owned by a `std::vector` local?
cards.a:
The vector's destructor, when the vector goes out of scope

Containers and smart pointers free their heap memory in their destructors. That is the RAII idea in lesson 2.04.
